tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Set up a boxd pool on a discobox server: make a new boxd API key with the
# boxd CLI, create (or update) a boxd provider named boxd with it, and create a
# pool named boxd on that provider.
#
# Usage: scripts/boxd-pool.sh [--name NAME] [--region REGION] [--base ID] [discobox flags...]
#
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh                                  # provider and pool "boxd", made in nyc
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --region fra                     # the boxd region, which the provider requires
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --base <boxd image or snapshot ID>
#
# Run `boxd login` first: boxd makes API keys only for an interactive session.
# Each run makes a new key, named <name>-<random>. When the provider already
# exists its config is replaced with the new key, keeping its region unless
# --region names one (a region cannot change while the provider has pools), and
# the key it held is left in boxd for you to revoke. Flags the script does not know (--server, --project,
# ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default: discobox on
# PATH) and $BOXD the boxd CLI (default: boxd on PATH).
#
# The provider has no controlPlaneUrl, so the server opens a channel to its pool
# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The key is the server's
# alone: the pool's machine authenticates as itself, and is given no key (ADR
# 26-11-11-080 §9). The server seals the key in the provider's row and never
# returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).
#
# The provider names its region and no endpoint: the driver asks boxd's home
# endpoint for the region's (ListRegions) and makes and lists its machines
# there, while the key exchange and account calls stay at the home endpoint
# (ADR 26-11-15-507 §3).
set -eu

name=boxd
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
boxd=${BOXD:-boxd}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,30p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
	*) set -- "$@" "$arg" ;;
	esac
done

for cli in "$boxd" "$discobox"; do
	command -v "$cli" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$cli is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }
done
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

# A new provider is made in nyc unless --region says otherwise; an existing one
# keeps its region. Decided before a key is made, so a refusal leaves none.
exists=0
if current=$("$discobox" "$@" -o json admin provider get "$name" 2>/dev/null); then
	exists=1
	if [ -z "$region" ]; then
		region=$(printf '%s' "$current" | jq -r '(.config | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) // {} | .driver.region // empty')
		if [ -z "$region" ]; then
			echo "provider $name has no region, which boxd now requires; delete it and its pools and run this again (docs/public/boxd.md, Upgrading a provider without a region)" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
	fi
fi
[ -n "$region" ] || region=nyc

suffix=$(od -An -N4 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')
key_name="$name-$suffix"
if ! out=$("$boxd" auth keys create "$key_name" 2>&1); then
	printf '%s\n' "$out" >&2
	echo "boxd did not make a key; run \`boxd login\` and try again" >&2
	exit 1
fi
key=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -oE 'bxd_[A-Za-z0-9_-]+' | head -1 || true)
if [ -z "$key" ]; then
	echo "boxd made key $key_name but printed no bxd_ key; revoke it in boxd" >&2
	exit 1
fi
echo "made boxd API key $key_name" >&2

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
jq -n --arg key "$key" --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: {apiKey: $key, region: $region}} + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null

#!/bin/sh
# Set up a boxd pool on a discobox server: make a new boxd API key with the
# boxd CLI, create (or update) a boxd provider named boxd with it, and create a
# pool named boxd on that provider.
#
# Usage: scripts/boxd-pool.sh [--name NAME] [--region REGION] [--base ID] [discobox flags...]
#
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh                                  # provider and pool "boxd", made in nyc
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --region fra                     # the boxd region, which the provider requires
#   scripts/boxd-pool.sh --base <boxd image or snapshot ID>
#
# Run `boxd login` first: boxd makes API keys only for an interactive session.
# Each run makes a new key, named <name>-<random>. When the provider already
# exists its config is replaced with the new key, keeping its region unless
# --region names one (a region cannot change while the provider has pools), and
# the key it held is left in boxd for you to revoke. Flags the script does not know (--server, --project,
# ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default: discobox on
# PATH) and $BOXD the boxd CLI (default: boxd on PATH).
#
# The provider has no controlPlaneUrl, so the server opens a channel to its pool
# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The key is the server's
# alone: the pool's machine authenticates as itself, and is given no key (ADR
# 26-11-11-080 §9). The server seals the key in the provider's row and never
# returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).
#
# The provider names its region and no endpoint: the driver asks boxd's home
# endpoint for the region's (ListRegions) and makes and lists its machines
# there, while the key exchange and account calls stay at the home endpoint
# (ADR 26-11-15-507 §3).
set -eu

name=boxd
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
boxd=${BOXD:-boxd}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,30p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
	*) set -- "$@" "$arg" ;;
	esac
done

for cli in "$boxd" "$discobox"; do
	command -v "$cli" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$cli is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }
done
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

# A new provider is made in nyc unless --region says otherwise; an existing one
# keeps its region. Decided before a key is made, so a refusal leaves none.
exists=0
if current=$("$discobox" "$@" -o json admin provider get "$name" 2>/dev/null); then
	exists=1
	if [ -z "$region" ]; then
		region=$(printf '%s' "$current" | jq -r '(.config | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) // {} | .driver.region // empty')
		if [ -z "$region" ]; then
			echo "provider $name has no region, which boxd now requires; delete it and its pools and run this again (docs/public/boxd.md, Upgrading a provider without a region)" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
	fi
fi
[ -n "$region" ] || region=nyc

suffix=$(od -An -N4 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')
key_name="$name-$suffix"
if ! out=$("$boxd" auth keys create "$key_name" 2>&1); then
	printf '%s\n' "$out" >&2
	echo "boxd did not make a key; run \`boxd login\` and try again" >&2
	exit 1
fi
key=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -oE 'bxd_[A-Za-z0-9_-]+' | head -1 || true)
if [ -z "$key" ]; then
	echo "boxd made key $key_name but printed no bxd_ key; revoke it in boxd" >&2
	exit 1
fi
echo "made boxd API key $key_name" >&2

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
jq -n --arg key "$key" --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: {apiKey: $key, region: $region}} + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

if [ "$exists" = 1 ]; then
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "updated provider $name with the new key; revoke the key it held before in boxd" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider create --type boxd --name "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "created provider $name in $region" >&2
fi

if "$discobox" "$@" admin pool get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "pool $name already exists" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin pool create "$name" --provider "$name" >/dev/null
	echo "created pool $name; watch it come up with: $discobox admin pool get $name" >&2
fi
echo "run a discobox on it with: $discobox run --pool $name" >&2

#!/bin/sh
# Set up an archil pool on a discobox server: create (or update) an archil
# provider named archil with an Archil API key, and create a pool named archil
# on that provider.
#
# Usage: scripts/archil-pool.sh [--name NAME] [--region REGION] [--base IMAGE] [discobox flags...]
#
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh                                # provider and pool "archil", in aws-us-east-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --region aws-eu-west-1         # aws-us-east-1, aws-us-west-2 or aws-eu-west-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --base debian:sid              # the public OCI image a fresh VM runs
#
# Archil has no CLI that makes keys: make one in the Archil console and pass it
# in $ARCHIL_API_KEY, or the script asks for it on the terminal without echoing
# it. When the provider already exists its config is replaced with the key,
# keeping its region unless --region names one (a region cannot change while
# the provider has pools). Flags the script does not know (--server,
# --project, ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default:
# discobox on PATH).
#
# The provider has no controlPlaneUrl, so the server opens a channel to its pool
# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The server seals the key
# in the provider's row and never returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).
#
# The server refuses a pool on archil for now: Archil has no machine isolation
# to fence a pool's sandboxes with (docs/public/concepts.md, VM providers). The
# provider is still made, and the pool's refusal is printed as the server says
# it.
set -eu

name=archil
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,28p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
	*) set -- "$@" "$arg" ;;
	esac
done

command -v "$discobox" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$discobox is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

# An existing provider keeps its region unless --region names one; a new one
# without --region is the driver's default.
exists=0
if current=$("$discobox" "$@" -o json admin provider get "$name" 2>/dev/null); then
	exists=1
	if [ -z "$region" ]; then
		region=$(printf '%s' "$current" | jq -r '(.config | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) // {} | .driver.region // empty')
	fi
fi

key=${ARCHIL_API_KEY:-}
if [ -z "$key" ]; then
	[ -t 0 ] || { echo "set ARCHIL_API_KEY to an API key from the Archil console" >&2; exit 2; }
	printf 'Archil API key: ' >&2
	stty -echo
	trap 'stty echo' EXIT INT TERM
	IFS= read -r key || true
	stty echo
	trap - EXIT INT TERM
	echo >&2
fi
key=$(printf '%s' "$key" | tr -d '[:space:]')
[ -n "$key" ] || { echo "no Archil API key given" >&2; exit 2; }

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key; the key reaches jq through its environment.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
ARCHIL_API_KEY=REDACTED jq -n --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: ({apiKey: $ENV.ARCHIL_API_KEY} + (if $region == "" then {} else {region: $region} end))}
	 + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

if [ "$exists" = 1 ]; then
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "updated provider $name with the key" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider create --type archil --name "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "created provider $name in ${region:-the default region (aws-us-east-1)}" >&2
fi

if "$discobox" "$@" admin pool get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "pool $name already exists" >&2
elif "$discobox" "$@" admin pool create "$name" --provider "$name" >/dev/null; then
	echo "created pool $name; watch it come up with: $discobox admin pool get $name" >&2
else
	echo "the server refused pool $name (above); provider $name is kept" >&2
	exit 1
fi
echo "run a discobox on it with: $discobox run --pool $name" >&2

I added `scripts/archil-pool.sh`, modelled on `boxd-pool.sh`. It creates a provider named `archil` (or updates it if it already exists) and then a pool of the same name on it.

**One thing to know first:** the server currently refuses pools on archil. `docs/public/concepts.md` says this is because Archil has no machine isolation, and the code check is in `server/providers/discovm/provider.go:190`. So for now the script will create the provider, but the pool step will fail with the server's own error message. It says the provider was kept and exits 1. Once that check is lifted, the same script will work all the way through.

How it differs from the boxd script:
- **API key:** Archil has no CLI that makes keys the way `boxd auth keys create` does. The script reads the key from `$ARCHIL_API_KEY`, or asks for it on the terminal without echoing it. As in the boxd script, the key goes to the CLI through a 0600 `@file`, never on the command line.
- **Region:** `--region` takes `aws-us-east-1` (the default), `aws-us-west-2` or `aws-eu-west-1`. If you leave it off, an existing provider keeps its region and a new one gets the default.
- **`--base`:** sets the public OCI image a fresh VM runs, e.g. `debian:sid`.
- `--name`, passing extra flags like `--server` through to `discobox`, and `$DISCOBOX` work the same as in the boxd script.

```sh
ARCHIL_API_KEY=key-... scripts/archil-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080

content.text:
`--server` isn't a flag of the script. It's the `discobox` CLI's global flag for choosing which discobox server to talk to (`cli/internal/cli/root.go:231`). The script doesn't recognise it, so it passes it, along with any other unknown flag, to every `discobox` call it makes.

It takes either an endpoint URL (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:8080`) or the name of a server you've registered with `discobox admin remote`. If you leave it off, the CLI uses `$DISCOBOX_SERVER` if that's set. Otherwise it uses the primary remote, or the local server if you haven't set a primary.

So the `--server http://127.0.0.1:8080` in the example just means "set up the provider and pool on the server at that address." For your usual server, leave it off.

# 26-10-31-694 — A provider's credentials are sealed in its row and never returned
Status: Accepted (§2's "a field the body leaves out keeps its sealed value" narrowed by [26-11-11-080](26-11-11-080-each-disco-vm-driver-is-a-provider-type-of-its-own-name-configured-by-its-own-fields.md) §4: a write that changes a `Privileged` driver field carries every secret field)
Date: 2026-10-31
## Context
A provider instance's credentials are stored and served in the clear. Four
config fields hold one — `digitalocean`'s `token` and `sshPrivateKey`,
`execvm`'s `sshPrivateKey`, and `vm`'s `apiKey` — and the instance's config is
one JSON column written as given (`store/providers.go`), with none of the
sealing a secret's value gets. The API returns the config with the key in it;
only the CLI hides it (`isSensitiveConfigKey`). Whoever reads the database, a
backup of it, or the provider over the API reads the key.
`providers/DESIGN.md` calls the config "non-secret", which these fields are
not. The row already has an `encrypted_config` column, which nothing writes.
Two more fields name an environment variable instead (`tokenEnv`,
`sshPrivateKeyEnv`): the key is whatever the server's process holds there.
The project's secrets store is the obvious place for a credential, and the
wrong one for these. Its secrets are what a person grants an agent: bound to
a discobox, a harness config or the project, requested, approved, delegated,
handed over raw ([ADR 26-10-27-880](26-10-27-880-access-to-a-secret-is-a-binding-held-to-static-routes-and-no-judge-decides-it.md)).
A provider's key is the setup of the pools agents run on. If it were a
project secret, a project member could bind it to a discobox, and an agent
would hold the key to every machine of the provider's account.
[ADR 26-10-16-470](26-10-16-470-a-project-may-route-a-providers-api-through-a-gateway.md)
kept a gateway's key out of the store for the same reason.
The vm provider's `deliverProviderKey` places its key on a pool's machine
([ADR 26-10-23-551](26-10-23-551-a-vm-pool-bootstraps-its-own-agent-from-a-bundle-and-provisions-its-machines.md)
§4). How it is delivered is unchanged here; where the key it delivers is
kept is not.
## Decision
### 1. A field the definition types `secret` is sealed in the provider's row
`sandbox.ProviderConfigField` gains the type `secret`. The four fields above
are typed `secret`, replacing `password`. A secret field's value is never in
the `config` column: the provider service moves the secret fields into
`encrypted_config`, a JSON object sealed with the store's sealer (the one a
secret's value is sealed with), and `config` keeps the rest.
- **The server joins them before the provider sees its config.** Resolving
  an instance opens `encrypted_config` and merges its fields into the
  config, which the provider decodes into the `Config` it decodes today.
  Validation runs on the merged config. A provider imports nothing of the
  store, and its code is unchanged except for the fields §6 removes.
- **No project secret is ever named.** A provider's credential is a field
  of that provider, not a reference to anything. It has no binding,
  appears in no secret listing, and no request, approval, delegation or raw
  binding reaches it. Nothing grants it to an agent, because it is not
  somewhere a grant can name.
- **Who sets one** is who may write the provider. Today that is a member of
  the provider's project, because there are no project roles. The provider
  routes are not in the sandbox role, so no discobox reads or writes one.
  When project roles exist, writing a provider (and so its credentials)
  belongs to the role that administers the project's pools.

# Encryption Design

`internal/encryption` seals what the server stores encrypted (ADR
26-11-02-902). It is discobox's use of `github.com/discobox-ai/envelope`:
each project's values are sealed with the project's own data key, and data
keys are stored only wrapped by the configured provider.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    config["config.EncryptionSettings (server.yaml encryption:)"] --> new[encryption.New]
    new --> provider["envelope provider: local, awskms, gcpkms, azurekeyvault, vaulttransit"]
    new --> keyring[Keyring]
    keyring --> envelope[envelope.Keyring]
    envelope -- "wrapped data keys" --> keys["store.EncryptionKeys (encryption_keys)"]
    store[internal/store] --> keyring
    auth["auth/sandbox, auth/poolagent"] --> keyring
```

- A `Field` names where a value lives: its scope (a project ID, or
  `ServerScope`), purpose, and resource ID. The scope picks the data key; the
  purpose and resource ID are the associated data, so a value's bytes do not
  open anywhere else. The constructors (`SecretValue`, ...) are the complete
  list of sealed fields; add one here when a column is sealed, and to
  `store.sealedColumns` so startup re-seals it.
- A nil `Keyring` is a server with no provider: values are stored unsealed,
  and a sealed one is an error rather than bytes passed through.
- `Open` reads every form a stored value has: `envelope:v1:`, `discobox:v1:`
  (sealed by a release before data keys with `encryptionKey`, opened with the
  local key or a retired one), and unsealed. `SealForWrite` stores any of
  them in the current format, verifying a sealed one against its field.
- `New` builds every provider from the SDK's own credential chain; Vault and
  OpenBao log in from the configuration. A Kubernetes login is renewed and
  repeated, and a `file:` token read again every 30s, until `Close`. A provider whose key cannot be reached fails
  `New`, so the server never starts on a misconfigured one.
- `encryption.local.key` opens what an earlier release sealed whichever
  provider is configured, so a server can move from `encryptionKey`
  straight to a KMS.
- `previous` adds an unwrap-only provider. The local provider's retired keys
  are unwrap-only too. Startup (`store.PrepareEncryption`) rewraps what
  either wrapped.

## Rules

- A scope's first key is made outside any transaction (`Ensure`): a key
  stored by a transaction that rolls back stays cached and seals values
  nothing can open later.
- Cloud credentials never come from the configuration file.

content.text:
The key is only ever stored on the server, encrypted, in the provider's row in the server's database. The script and CLI don't keep a copy.

1. **The script** reads `$ARCHIL_API_KEY`, or the hidden prompt, and writes it into a 0600 temp file made by `mktemp`. That file is deleted when the script exits. The key reaches `jq` through its environment, so it never appears on a command line where `ps` could see it.
2. **The CLI** reads that file (`--config @file`) and sends the key to the server in the body of the provider create or update request.
3. **The server** stores it encrypted, per ADR 26-10-31-694:
   - It moves the `driver.apiKey` field out of the provider's plain `config` column and into `encrypted_config`, sealed with the project's data key.
   - That data key is stored only wrapped by the server's encryption provider, set in `server.yaml` under `encryption:`. The options are local key, AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault and Vault/OpenBao (`server/internal/encryption/DESIGN.md`).
   - The API never returns the key, and project secrets and agent bindings can't reach it.
   - The server decrypts it only in memory, to call Archil's API.

**One caveat:** if your server has no encryption provider configured, the value is stored as base64 of the plaintext rather than encrypted. I haven't checked how your server is configured. Look for an `encryption:` section in its `server.yaml`.

The variable also stays in your own shell if you exported it. Running it as a one-off prefix, `ARCHIL_API_KEY=key-... scripts/archil-pool.sh`, avoids that.

#!/bin/sh
# Set up an archil pool on a discobox server: create (or update) an archil
# provider named archil with an Archil API key, and create a pool named archil
# on that provider.
#
# Usage: scripts/archil-pool.sh [--name NAME] [--region REGION] [--base IMAGE] [discobox flags...]
#
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh                                # provider and pool "archil", in aws-us-east-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --region aws-eu-west-1         # aws-us-east-1, aws-us-west-2 or aws-eu-west-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --base debian:sid              # the public OCI image a fresh VM runs
#
# Archil has no CLI that makes keys: make one in the Archil console and pass it
# in $ARCHIL_API_KEY, or the script asks for it on the terminal without echoing
# it. When the provider already exists its config is replaced with the key,
# keeping its region unless --region names one (a region cannot change while
# the provider has pools). Flags the script does not know (--server,
# --project, ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default:
# discobox on PATH).
#
# The provider has no controlPlaneUrl, so the server opens a channel to its pool
# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The server seals the key
# in the provider's row and never returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).
#
# The server refuses a pool on archil for now: Archil has no machine isolation
# to fence a pool's sandboxes with (docs/public/concepts.md, VM providers). The
# provider is still made, and the pool's refusal is printed as the server says
# it.
set -eu

name=archil
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;
	-h|--help) sed -n '2,28p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
	*) set -- "$@" "$arg" ;;
	esac
done

command -v "$discobox" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$discobox is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "jq is not on PATH" >&2; exit 2; }

# An existing provider keeps its region unless --region names one; a new one
# without --region is the driver's default.
exists=0
if current=$("$discobox" "$@" -o json admin provider get "$name" 2>/dev/null); then
	exists=1
	if [ -z "$region" ]; then
		region=$(printf '%s' "$current" | jq -r '(.config | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) // {} | .driver.region // empty')
	fi
fi

key=${ARCHIL_API_KEY:-}
if [ -z "$key" ]; then
	[ -t 0 ] || { echo "set ARCHIL_API_KEY to an API key from the Archil console" >&2; exit 2; }
	printf 'Archil API key: ' >&2
	stty -echo
	trap 'stty echo' EXIT INT TERM
	IFS= read -r key || true
	stty echo
	trap - EXIT INT TERM
	echo >&2
fi
key=$(printf '%s' "$key" | tr -d '[:space:]')
[ -n "$key" ] || { echo "no Archil API key given" >&2; exit 2; }

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key; the key reaches jq through its environment.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
ARCHIL_API_KEY=REDACTED jq -n --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: ({apiKey: $ENV.ARCHIL_API_KEY} + (if $region == "" then {} else {region: $region} end))}
	 + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

if [ "$exists" = 1 ]; then
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "updated provider $name with the key" >&2
else
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider create --type archil --name "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null
	echo "created provider $name in ${region:-the default region (aws-us-east-1)}" >&2
fi

if "$discobox" "$@" admin pool get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "pool $name already exists" >&2
elif "$discobox" "$@" admin pool create "$name" --provider "$name" >/dev/null; then
	echo "created pool $name; watch it come up with: $discobox admin pool get $name" >&2
else
	echo "the server refused pool $name (above); provider $name is kept" >&2
	exit 1
fi
echo "run a discobox on it with: $discobox run --pool $name" >&2

content.text:
I fixed the script so it always sends a region. The vm module the server is now built with requires one; the older copy I read when writing the script treated it as optional.

- With no `--region`, a new provider is created in `aws-us-east-1`.
- An existing provider keeps its own region. If it was made before regions were required, it gets `aws-us-east-1`, which is where the server says those providers' VMs already are.
- `--region aws-eu-west-1` or `--region aws-us-west-2` picks one of the others.

I tested it against a stub `discobox`: it now sends `{"driver":{"apiKey":"…","region":"aws-us-east-1"}}`. I haven't run it against your server, so re-run it there. If it gets past the provider step, the pool step may still be refused because Archil has no machine isolation, unless that check has changed in your current build too.

# provider named archil with an Archil API key, and create a pool named archil
# on that provider.

#
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh                                # provider and pool "archil", in aws-us-east-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --server http://127.0.0.1:8080
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --region aws-eu-west-1         # aws-us-east-1, aws-us-west-2 or aws-eu-west-1
#   scripts/archil-pool.sh --base debian:sid              # the public OCI image a fresh VM runs

# it. When the provider already exists its config is replaced with the key,
# keeping its region unless --region names one (a region cannot change while
# the provider has pools). The driver requires a region; without --region a
# new provider is made in aws-us-east-1. Flags the script does not know (--server,
# --project, ...) go to every discobox call; $DISCOBOX names the CLI (default:
# discobox on PATH).

# machine and needs no public URL (ADR 26-10-30-875). The server seals the key
# in the provider's row and never returns it (ADR 26-10-31-694).

# to fence a pool's sandboxes with (docs/public/concepts.md, VM providers). The
# provider is still made, and the pool's refusal is printed as the server says
# it.

name=archil
region=
base=
discobox=${DISCOBOX:-discobox}
# The script's flags may come anywhere; the rest are rotated to the back of
# "$@", in order, for discobox.
n=$#
while [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; do
	arg=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
	case $arg in
	--name|--region|--base)
		[ "$n" -gt 0 ] || { echo "$arg needs a value" >&2; exit 2; }
		val=$1; shift; n=$((n - 1))
		case $arg in
		--name) name=$val ;;
		--region) region=$val ;;
		*) base=$val ;;
		esac ;;
	--name=*) name=${arg#*=} ;;
	--region=*) region=${arg#*=} ;;
	--base=*) base=${arg#*=} ;;

if [ -z "$region" ]; then
	found=0
	for r in aws-us-east-1 aws-us-west-2 aws-eu-west-1; do
		host=control.green.${r#aws-}.aws.prod.archil.com
		code=$(printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer key-%s"\n' "${key#key-}" |
			curl -sS -m 20 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -K - \
				-H 'Accept: application/json' "https://$host/api/sandboxes") || code=000
		case $code in
		2??) region=$r; found=$((found + 1)) ;;
		401|403) ;;
		*) echo "archil $r answered $code; name the key's region with --region" >&2; exit 1 ;;
		esac
	done
	case $found in
	0) echo "no Archil region takes that key (aws-us-east-1, aws-us-west-2, aws-eu-west-1)" >&2; exit 1 ;;
	1) echo "the key is for $region" >&2 ;;
	*) echo "more than one Archil region takes that key; name one with --region" >&2; exit 1 ;;
	esac
fi

exists=0
"$discobox" "$@" admin provider get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 && exists=1

# The config goes to the CLI as @file, never on a command line, where other
# users' ps would read the key; the key reaches jq through its environment.
config=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$config"' EXIT
chmod 600 "$config"
ARCHIL_API_KEY=REDACTED jq -n --arg region "$region" --arg base "$base" \
	'{driver: {apiKey: $ENV.ARCHIL_API_KEY, region: $region}}
	 + (if $base == "" then {} else {base: $base} end)' >"$config"

if [ "$exists" = 1 ]; then
	"$discobox" "$@" admin provider update "$name" --config "@$config" >/dev/null

else

	echo "created provider $name in $region" >&2
fi

if "$discobox" "$@" admin pool get "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "pool $name already exists" >&2
elif "$discobox" "$@" admin pool create "$name" --provider "$name" >/dev/null; then
	echo "created pool $name; watch it come up with: $discobox admin pool get $name" >&2
else
	echo "the server refused pool $name (above); provider $name is kept" >&2
	exit 1
fi
echo "run a discobox on it with: $discobox run --pool $name" >&2

Yes, and the script now does it. Archil has no API that reports a key's region, but each region has its own control plane, and an invalid key gets a 401 from all three. So without `--region`, the script sends the key to each region's control plane (a sandbox listing, the same call the driver makes) and uses the one region that accepts it.

- **No region accepts the key:** it stops with "no Archil region takes that key".
- **More than one accepts it** (which shouldn't happen): it asks you to pass `--region`.
- **A region gives an unexpected answer** (not success, 401 or 403), or can't be reached: it stops and tells you to pass `--region`, rather than guess.
- **`--region`** still works and skips the check.
- **Existing provider:** it gets the found region along with the new key. The server refuses a region change while the provider has pools, so a mismatched key fails there rather than silently.

The key is passed to `curl` on stdin (`-K -`), so it never appears on a command line. The script also rejects a key containing a quote or backslash, because those would break `curl`'s config syntax.

**Tested so far:** an invalid key gets "no Archil region takes that key", and `--region` builds the right config against a stub `discobox`. **Not tested:** that a valid key is accepted only in its own region. I don't have a real key, so the first real run with yours will be the test. It should print "the key is for aws-…" before creating the provider.

## Create a pool and run a box

```sh
discobox admin pool create boxd --provider boxd
discobox admin pool get boxd
discobox run --pool boxd
```

The pool is ready when `admin pool get` shows it `active`. The first box of a
kind (its harness and setup) provisions from scratch, and takes longest.
Behind it, the pool builds a snapshot of that kind on a machine of its own;
boxes of that kind made once the snapshot is ready start from it. Make the
pool the project's default with `discobox admin pool set-default boxd`.

Before it makes a pool's machine, the server checks the account through
boxd's API: that the key is accepted, that the org has the provider's region
enabled, and that no host-bound secret is in the org or the key owner's
personal scope. The pool fails with the reason if boxd refuses, and waits if
boxd does not answer. A running pool's account is checked again every ten
minutes, which reads the org's machine limit: the pool's `runtime` condition
shows it as `maxMachines`, counting every machine billed to the org, stopped
ones and other members' included. A check that fails then is logged, and the
pool keeps running.

## What the key can reach

See [Bundle Assets](#bundle-assets). |
pool-agent/DESIGN.md:32:| `sandboxruntime` | The `Runtime` interface and its implementations (`DockerSandboxRuntime`; `MachineSandboxRuntime`, a machine pool's, see [Machine Sandboxes](#machine-sandboxes); `MemorySandboxRuntime` for tests). What does not depend on what a sandbox runs as is `sandboxCore`, which both real runtimes embed: the per-sandbox records in its tree, the runtime-config document and its delivery, the power lock and boot mark, the state and progress sinks, sources' settling, proxy policy staging and the credentials broker's environment (`publishCredentialEnvironment`, from the pool's file-secrets record), the Git cache and the agent layer's extraction. It asks the runtime it is embedded in, through the unexported `boxes` interface, only what that runtime alone knows: how to find, reach, wait for and rebuild a sandbox's box. `Runtime` is everything the agent needs from a runtime — sandbox CRUD and power (a delete also taking the sandbox's audit trail from the proxy, through the `AuditPurger` `sandboxCore` holds), the durable tree, origin paths, how the pool reaches a sandbox ([Reaching a Sandbox](#reaching-a-sandbox)), the state channel, what its own store holds of the pool's disk (`DiskUsage`), the pool's snapshots as its resource report carries them (`Snapshots`, [Reporting](#reporting)), and the tree and proxy-material reclaim loops — so `Serve` holds no concrete type and a second runtime is a drop-in (ADR 0144 §2). What only a Docker pool has, such as image reclamation (`WatchImages`), stays on the Docker type and is started by the Docker pool's composition in `RunAgent`. The Docker runtime implements the durable-tree export and restore a transfer moves (ADR 0123; `tree.go`). ## Create a pool and run a box

```sh
discobox admin pool create boxd --provider boxd
discobox admin pool get boxd
discobox run --pool boxd
```

The pool is ready when `admin pool get` shows it `active`. The first box of a
kind (its harness and setup) provisions from scratch, and takes longest.
Behind it, the pool builds a snapshot of that kind on a machine of its own;
boxes of that kind made once the snapshot is ready start from it. Make the
pool the project's default with `discobox admin pool set-default boxd`.

Before it makes a pool's machine, the server checks the account through
boxd's API: that the key is accepted, that the org has the provider's region
enabled, and that no host-bound secret is in the org or the key owner's
personal scope. The pool fails with the reason if boxd refuses, and waits if
boxd does not answer. A running pool's account is checked again every ten
minutes, which reads the org's machine limit: the pool's `runtime` condition
shows it as `maxMachines`, counting every machine billed to the org, stopped
ones and other members' included. A check that fails then is logged, and the
pool keeps running.

## Snapshots A delivered create starts from a **snapshot** of its plan when the pool has one, and otherwise from its base, provisioning from scratch as above while the snapshot is built behind it ([ADR 26-10-16-423](../docs/adr/26-10-16-423-a-harness-is-a-provisioning-bundle-and-the-agent-provisions-any-box.md) §8, [ADR 26-11-03-986](../docs/adr/26-11-03-986-a-machine-pool-snapshots-a-plan-by-committing-a-vm-it-provisioned-and-shut-down.md); `snapshot.go`, shared by both runtimes). A snapshot is only a cache: the control plane is told what the pool holds and which a box started from ([Reporting](#reporting)) and decides nothing from it, and nothing fails for want of one. A Docker pool's snapshot is a committed image (`snapshotdocker.go`); a machine pool's is a committed disco-vm VM, and only where its driver reports `Capabilities.Commit` ([On a machine pool](#on-a-machine-pool)). ```mermaid flowchart LR create["delivered create"] --> key["plan key: base, project, pool,
agent, pins, features off, provisionEgress"] key -->|"a snapshot of the plan"| snap["start from the snapshot"] key -->|"none"| base["start from the base"] --> ask["build it in the background
(one at a time; a failure waits an hour)"] ask --> build["build box: base + agent layer + pins"] build -->|"exec: discobox-sandbox-agent snapshot, SnapshotPlan on stdin
(provisions, every feature done, cleans, seals)"| stop["stop in order"] stop --> commit["commit"] ``` - **The build is one exec** (`runSnapshotCommand`, through `provisioner.Provision` on both runtimes: a container as `provisioner.ContainerGuest`). The taker starts its box, places the agent, its units and its pins, and runs the agent's `snapshot` command as one blocking exec with the plan on its stdin, whose exit status and stderr are the build's result. The command refuses to seal a box with any feature not done or failed (as `discobox-provision wait` reads it), so no snapshot is committed that is not provisioned whole. The guest never powers itself off: the taker stops the box in order and commits it. - **The key** (`snapshotPlan`) is everything the snapshot holds depends on and nothing of the sandbox: the base (a Docker pool's sandbox base image ID; a machine pool's driver and the base its configuration names), the agent it is placed with and its bundles in order, the features turned off, and the create's `provisionEgress`. Every sandbox of one plan shares one snapshot. - **A build is anonymous.** Its proxy identity is its own (`layout.SnapshotIDPrefix`), with a client certificate, and an asset record of the plan's pins in its own tree, `layout.Root.Snapshot` — never a sandbox's tree, so neither the control plane nor any sandbox sweep sees it — and the egress policy the server sends as `provisionEgress`: every level of ADR 26-10-01-032 but the sandbox's own. Its `agentlayer.SnapshotPlan` names no account, source, secret, gateway, sentinel or credentials endpoint. The material reaper leaves a build's identity alone, since it has no sandbox container to be found by: its material goes with the build, or with the sweep once its container is gone. - **Nothing of the build is committed but what it provisioned.** The plan, which holds the build's client key, is never on a disk: it is the command's stdin. Its proxy material and the agent's record of it are under `/etc/discobox`, which is never on the committed disk either — a Docker build's bind, a VM build's tmpfs the command mounts in systemd's own mount namespace, entering it first where the exec runs in another (boxd's) — and which the command empties before it returns. It empties `machine-id`, removes SSH host keys, gives back the provider's resolver its DNS stub took over (and the record of it), takes the build's proxy CA back out of the trust store, and writes the seal (`agentlayer.SealedFile`): a box made from a snapshot gives itself a new machine ID and SSH host keys when its bootstrap arrives, before anything else, since a boot the pool did not run (boxd's commit boots the disk once more) may have written them again. It removes the agent's start link, so a box made from the snapshot starts its agent when its maker says, as a fresh one does, and the re-execution for the new machine ID never runs under the maker's own systemctl calls. A container inherits its image's labels, so the build carries only its project's and pool's, which every container of the pool carries, and none saying it is a build, which would mark every sandbox started from the snapshot. It is found by its name (`snapshotContainerPrefix`) with those labels: one no build under way holds — left by an agent that stopped mid-build, maybe still running — is swept with its tree and proxy material by the image reclaim, so none provisions on under a policy the pool no longer keeps, and it is removed with its pool by `SyncKnownPools`. - **A build is a start.** On a Docker pool it enters the pool's start gate for its whole length, and a cache clear ends it once the gate is shut ([Clearing the Pool's Caches](#clearing-the-pools-caches)). On either, a clear forgets the plans that failed. - **A plan whose build failed waits an hour** before a create asks again. Its failure is kept in the pool's tree (`snapshot-failures/`), not in memory, so an agent that keeps restarting does not keep building: a JSON record of when, why (the build's error, bounded, its middle elided) and the plan. A bare time, as a pool before it wrote, reads as a failure with no reason and no plan. - **A create with no `provisionEgress`** — from a server before it — starts from the base and builds nothing, rather than building unrestricted. - **The snapshot** is tagged `discobox-snapshot:` and labelled with the base it was built from (`snapshotBaseLabel`), the agent layer it holds (`snapshotAgentLabel`), its plan as the pool reports it (`snapshotPlanLabel`) and the reclaim label (ADR 0040), so an unused one ages out like any Discobox image. One built on an older base is no snapshot of the plan. `deliveredMoved` reads a snapshot's base as its container's, so a moved pin still restarts a box started from one, and `placeAgent` places no layer the snapshot already holds. - **What a build mounts** is its own tree's bound directory and nothing of a sandbox's: no primary volume, no pool cache, no declared volume. It provisions onto the root filesystem the snapshot keeps, as an image is built: content a step installs under a declared `data` path is image content the box's wiring overlays (ADR 0007 §3), and one under a `cache` path, which a plain bind hides, is the step's to ship aside, as `nix` does. Its bound directory is in the pool's data subtree, beside the sandboxes' trees (`layout.Root.PoolSnapshots`), never in the build area no box may reach (ADR 0050). - **The build's contract is the agent's**, not a runtime's: the agent's `snapshot` command run as an exec, `agentlayer.SnapshotPlan` on its stdin, and the seal. What a runtime adds is its box — a Docker pool's container, with the bind that keeps `SnapshotDir` out of what payload — `observedAt` and `resources` — and the payload itself is still forwarded as received, never re-serialized from a parsed structure, so a field this agent does not model still reaches the control plane. The computed figures travel in this agent's own report, never merged into the sandbox-agent's. **The pool's snapshots ride every report** (`snapshots`, from `Runtime.Snapshots`): an image list and a few small records, cheap enough for the tick rather than the sweep ([Reporting](#reporting)). **Both loops share one poll.** The resource reporter reads the counters the status poller already collected (`sandboxAgentStatusPoller.ResourceSamples`) rather than polling each sandbox a second time for the same two numbers. **Attribution reaches processes.** Each sandbox offers a candidate list — the union of the busiest by cumulative CPU and the largest by RSS — and this agent differences them per `(pid, startTicks)` and keeps the top few by *rate*. The start time is in the key because PIDs are reused; without it a recycled PID differences into a spike that never happened. Ranking by the cumulative counter would put a day-old language server above a test run that has just started eating the box. **Disk is two measurements on two schedules.** `statfs` on `/var/lib/discobox` is one syscall and rides every report — it is the figure that answers "is this pool about to fill up". Per-tree attribution is one pass over every inode the pool owns and runs on `storageScanner`'s own adaptive schedule; the report never a caller-supplied one, so this endpoint can never be used to obtain a broader sandbox-agent token. `ReportSandboxAgentStatus` and `ReportPoolResources` write their sandbox columns through narrow column updates (`store.UpdateSandboxAgentStatus`, `store.UpdateSandboxResources`), not `UpdateSandbox`/`WithGeneration` — this telemetry is outside the desired/observed generation contract and a whole-row save would risk clobbering concurrent desired-state writes. Agent status also moves a sandbox's `LastActiveAt` forward from the reported session access, and records the reported `meta` through `store.UpdateSandboxMeta` (ADR 0136); a report without it leaves the recorded copy alone. `ReportPoolResources` stores the pool-wide half on the pool row and each sandbox's half on that sandbox's row; the pool's snapshots ride the pool-wide half, stored as reported and read by nothing on the server ([ADR 26-11-17-316](../../../../docs/adr/26-11-17-316-a-pool-reports-its-snapshots-and-each-box-what-it-started-from.md) §4). A state observation's `startedFrom` (§5) is stored in the client-facing `SandboxStartedFrom` shape, and one that omits it hands on nothing, so the recorded value stands. `ReconcilePool` (a manual reconcile request from the API) also lives here. - `controlplane.go` — trusted operations implementing `sandbox.PoolManager`: reads for drivers, enrollment (`EnrollPool`: the key a pool's maker read from its box, ADR 26-10-24-953 §4), what a pool's box is placed with

lastPrompt: while a snapshot is building for a discobox is there progress reported anywhere for it?

content.text:
You can see whether a build is queued or running and when it started, but not how far along it is. Nothing reports progress within a build.

**`discobox admin pool get <pool>`** is the main place to look. It shows a `SNAPSHOTS` summary line (e.g. `1 held, 1 building, 0 failed`) and then one row per snapshot:

```
SNAPSHOT      STATE     WHEN              PLAN                 DETAIL
3f9a1c2e7b04  building  started 4m ago    claude-code@ab12…
```

- `STATE` is one of:
  - `queued`: asked for, but waiting behind another build, since a pool runs one build at a time.
  - `building`: running.
  - `held`: done; DETAIL shows its size, how many boxes use it and when it was last used.
  - `failed`: DETAIL shows the error and when a new create may try again (failed builds wait an hour).
- `-o json` has the full record (`resources.snapshots.building[]` with `requestedAt`/`startedAt`).
- This comes from the pool's resource report, so it refreshes on each report tick rather than live (ADR 26-11-17-316, `cli/internal/cli/pool_snapshots.go`).

**`discobox admin pool logs <pool> --follow`** shows the pool agent's own log lines: `building a snapshot`, then `built a snapshot … took=…` or the failure with its error (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/snapshot.go:218-243`). That tells you when a build starts and ends, but nothing in between.

**`discobox ls`** has a `STARTED FROM` column, which says whether each box started from a snapshot (and which one) or from the base.

The build itself is one blocking exec of the sandbox agent's `snapshot` command. Only its exit status and stderr come back, and only as the result, so feature-by-feature provisioning progress isn't streamed anywhere. Meanwhile the box that triggered the build is provisioning from scratch on its own, and its progress shows normally, since that's the box's own provisioning rather than the snapshot's. Adding per-step progress would mean streaming the exec's output, or a progress field in the `building` record.

## discobox admin pool console

~~~~text
Open an administrative console on the machine hosting a pool's runtime.

The console is a privileged container in the pool host's PID, IPC, network,
UTS, and cgroup namespaces, running as root with the host filesystem at /host
and the host's Docker socket in place. It runs the pool image, so docker, git,
and curl are already there.

It is meant for debugging a backend — a WSL or macOS VM that will not boot
Docker, an agent that never registers — and reaches the host through the
provider driver rather than through the pool agent, so it still answers when
the agent does not.

A vm pool has no such container: on a remote driver the console is a login shell
in the pool's machine, and on a local one there is none to open, because the
pool agent runs on this machine itself — read its log with "discobox admin pool
logs" instead.

One console container is kept per pool host and reattached, so a capture or a
trace started in it survives a detach. The shell exits when you type exit, and
the next console starts a fresh one.

The command follows POOL; an optional -- separates them explicitly.
Use a leading -- to omit POOL and use the default pool.
CLI flags go before POOL; everything after it is passed to the command.
Stdin is attached, stdout and stderr stay separate without a TTY, and the
command's exit status is returned.
A TTY is allocated when stdin is a terminal, or with -t; TTY output is merged.
One-off commands have the same host access and do not change the persistent shell.

Without POOL the project's default pool is used.

content.text:
There's no CLI command that streams a snapshot build's log. The pool agent only gets the build's output when it finishes: the tail of stderr, and only on failure. That's what appears in `admin pool get` and `admin pool logs`.

While a build runs, the log lives inside the build box. The build provisions each feature with the same runner a normal box uses, and each feature writes to `/var/log/discobox/provision/<feature>.log` (`sandbox-agent/provision/box.go:15`). To watch it, get a shell in the build box:

**Docker pool:** the build is a container on the pool host called `discobox-snapshot-<poolID>-<id>`.
```sh
discobox admin pool console <pool>          # root shell on the pool host, with its Docker socket
docker ps --filter name=discobox-snapshot-
docker exec -it <container> sh -c 'tail -F /var/log/discobox/provision/*.log'
```

**VM pool (boxd):** the build is a machine whose name starts with `snap-` followed by the first 24 characters of the plan key (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/machinesnapshot.go:52`). Find it in `boxd machine list`, then:
```sh
boxd machine exec <snap-machine> -- sh -c 'tail -F /var/log/discobox/provision/*.log'
```
`discobox admin pool console <pool>` also works here: on a remote driver it gives a login shell on the pool's machine. I haven't confirmed that boxd shows the build machine under exactly that `snap-` name, so check the list.

Inside the box, `/run/discobox/provision` (the status file `discobox-provision wait` reads) shows which features are done, running or failed.

Two catches:
- Grab the logs before the build ends. On success the box is stopped and committed; on failure it's removed. Afterwards, only the stderr tail in the `failed` row of `admin pool get` is left.
- The box that triggered the build is provisioning the same features from scratch at the same time, and its logs are easier to reach: `discobox exec <box> -- tail -F /var/log/discobox/provision/*.log`. It's usually the quickest way to see what the snapshot is doing, though it's a separate run, not the build's own output.

If you want this in the product, the natural fix would be to stream the build exec's output into the pool agent's log, or expose the build box's feature logs through `admin pool get`. I can sketch either.

The archil pool is healthy, and one snapshot build has been running for about 17 minutes. I couldn't get into the build machine to watch its log, so I can't tell whether it's progressing or stuck.

**Pool** (`discobox admin pool get archil`): active, ready, schedulable. Snapshots: 0 held, 1 building, 0 failed. The build `9a38cdc18f15` (Claude Code plan) started at 18:06:36 UTC.

**Pool log** (`discobox admin pool logs archil`):
- **18:06:05:** Archil refused the key (`Unauthorized (401)`) on several machine listings. After 18:06:15 those errors stop, so the key or region was presumably fixed then.
- **18:06:36:** `building a snapshot`. Nothing since then reports how it's going, which is expected because the build only reports when it ends.
- **18:06:37–18:07:07:** an `http: proxy error: EOF` line every two seconds, then it stopped. This lines up with the build machine coming up, but I haven't confirmed the cause.
- **18:22:** `rejected a control-plane request … no sandbox token` on git-origin fetches for `sbx_avnbbz379tkqjgc1`. Its sources still show as delivered, so this was probably harmless retries. I haven't checked further.

**Boxes on the pool** (all started from the base, none from a snapshot yet):

| Box | Created (UTC) | State |
|---|---|---|
| `sbx_1yndtkc0jshhvm94` | ~18:05 | error: "archil: list sandboxes: the key was refused". This is from the 401 window; it never got a machine. Delete it. |
| `sbx_74pw9ze1vesshxzb` | ~18:06 | running, every feature ready |
| `sbx_avnbbz379tkqjgc1` | 18:20:51 | running, still provisioning `desktop`, `direnv` and `mise` |

**The build's own logs:** I couldn't reach them. `discobox admin pool console archil` gets a shell on the pool's machine. Its Archil tools only manage the machine they run on, and the pool agent's environment holds no key I could reuse. `ARCHIL_API_KEY` isn't set in this shell either.

To watch the build, find its sandbox in the Archil console. It should have the pool's `dvm-` name prefix and `snap-` in its name, though I haven't seen it to confirm. Then tail `/var/log/discobox/provision/*.log` in it.

17 minutes may be normal. The plan includes heavy features (nix, docker, desktop), and `sbx_avnbbz379tkqjgc1` is still provisioning some of the same features from the base. If it hasn't finished in the next 15–20 minutes, it's probably stuck; I can check again then.

Manage discoboxes

Usage:
  discobox admin box [command] [flags]

Aliases:
  box, boxes

Commands:
  ls, list              List discoboxes
  get                   Show a discobox
  create                Create a discobox
  update                Update a discobox
  rm, delete, remove    Archive a discobox
  unarchive             Restore an archived discobox
  purge                 Destroy a discobox and its data
  start                 Start a discobox
  stop                  Stop a discobox
  restart               Restart a discobox
  pause                 Pause a discobox, keeping its memory
  repair                Repair a discobox by rebuilding it on the current image
  reprovision           Run a discobox's failed provisioning again, in place
  upgrade               Upgrade a discobox to its harness config's current image
  resources, top        Show what a discobox is consuming
  export                Write a discobox to a portable archive
  import                Create a discobox from a portable archive
  transfer              Move a discobox to another server

Options:
  -h, --help           help for box

Global options:
      --color WHEN     set color WHEN to auto, always, or never (default auto)
      --debug          print HTTP requests and the git commands run on this machine
  -o, --output FORMAT  output FORMAT: table or json (default table)
      --server SERVER  connect to SERVER, an endpoint or a registered server's name; defaults to the primary "discobox admin remote primary" set, and to the local server when none is
      --token TOKEN    bearer TOKEN for API requests

Use "discobox admin box [command] --help" for more information about a command.
## Today

On an archil pool, the machine that builds a plan's snapshot never reaches the pool, so the snapshot never finishes. Seen live on 2026-11-23, on main `6ee7a0a` (with #1563), Archil aws-us-east-1:
- `scripts/live-run.sh --driver archil`: `FAIL snapshot: no held snapshot after 30m: []`. The pool reports the plan's snapshot as `building` for the whole 30m.
- A second pool: the `snap-<key>` machine is `running` after 10 minutes. Its journal shows the sandbox proxy bridge failing every 50s from boot:

```
ERROR sandbox proxy bridge could not reach the pool proxy worker=wss://7302-<pool host>.prod-aws-us-east-1-green.archil.app/tunnel/proxy error="… dial tcp: lookup 7302-<pool host>.prod-aws-us-east-1-green.archil.app. on 169.254.53.53:53: read udp …->8.8.8.8:53: i/o timeout … ->1.1.1.1:53: i/o timeout"
```

A discobox on the same pool reaches the pool fine. Its `/etc/discobox/proxy/bridge.json` has `edgePath` and `credentialsUrl`. The snapshot builder's has neither (keys only; values redacted):

```
sandbox:  {listenAddress, workerProxyUrl, serverName, edgePath, credentialsUrl, dnsSystemResolver, dnsServer, dnsListenAddress, mtlsCaPath, clientCertPath, clientKeyPath}
snapshot: {listenAddress, workerProxyUrl, serverName,                         dnsSystemResolver, dnsServer, dnsListenAddress, mtlsCaPath, clientCertPath, clientKeyPath}
```

So the builder's bridge doesn't take the edge path that dials the pool without DNS (ADR 26-11-16-619 §3, #1286). It resolves the pool's host instead, and the fence denies the guest's resolvers.

## Wanted

A snapshot-build machine on a pool fenced at its provider's edge gets the same edge placement as a sandbox machine (the edge path, the credential and the pool's address), so it reaches the pool with DNS closed and its build completes.

## Done when

On archil (fake API, and live by #1060's run), a plan's snapshot reaches `held`, and a second discobox starts from it.

Found while working on #1060.

content.text:
I filed it as **https://github.com/discobox-ai/discobox/issues/1597**, labelled `type/feature`, `area/cli`, `area/pool-agent` and `priority/medium`.

The issue asks for:
- **A listing of builds:** for example `discobox admin box ls --snapshots`, or a flag on `discobox ls`, showing each running build's pool, plan key, state and what it runs in. It would be read from the pool's report, because builds deliberately have no sandbox row (ADR 26-11-17-316).
- **Progress:** each build's per-feature provisioning status (state, step, error), the way a box already reports it, so you can see where it's stuck without a shell.
- **Logs and a shell:** following a build's feature logs and running commands in it through the CLI, without provider credentials. This matters most on archil, where the pool's console can't reach the build machine.
- **Optionally, keeping a failed build:** leaving a failed build's box around for a while so its logs can still be read.

It's done when all of that works while a build runs, on a Docker pool and on an archil or boxd pool.

Your current build is likely hitting **#1585**, which is already open: "An archil pool's snapshot build never reaches the pool". The build machine's proxy bridge can't reach the pool because it has no edge path. That issue describes builds sitting in `building` for 30 minutes, which fits what we're seeing. The issue only says "likely", since nothing in discobox could confirm it, which is the gap #1597 is about.

content.text:
That log line confirms it: this build is stuck on **#1585**.

It's the same error #1585 records. The build machine's proxy bridge tries to reach the pool by resolving `7302-<pool host>.prod-aws-us-west-2-green.archil.app`. It asks `8.8.8.8` and `1.1.1.1` through the guest's resolver (`169.254.53.53`), and both time out because the pool's fence blocks the guest's DNS. A normal box on this pool doesn't need DNS here: it's given the edge path and credentials URL. The build machine's `bridge.json` doesn't get them, so it can never reach the pool proxy, and it can't fetch bundles or finish provisioning.

What this means for you:
- **This build won't finish.** It stays `building` until it times out. After a failure, the plan waits an hour before a new box asks for another build.
- **Boxes still work.** New boxes keep starting from the base and provisioning from scratch, as `sbx_74pw9ze1vesshxzb` did. They just don't get the snapshot speed-up.
- **The fix is #1585,** which is already `status/in-progress`. The build machine needs the same edge placement a box gets.

This also adds to #1585: it now reproduces in `aws-us-west-2`, not just `us-east-1`. The pool's region came from the key, so `archil-pool.sh` chose `aws-us-west-2`. Want me to add this log line to #1585 as a comment?
